01 — Why it matters

Separation is a soldering process you are running without a recipe

A panel that has passed reflow, wave solder, AOI and test carries fully paid-for value. The depaneling step is the only station where a good assembly can still become scrap — and it is usually the station with the least written-down process. Snapping, breaking and hand-cutting depend on how strong the operator's wrist is that shift. The board does not know the difference between a designed break and an accident; it only knows the stress.

01

Micro-cracks appear after the split, not during it

Mechanical snapping loads the panel in bending. The panel survives it, so the line records no defect. Weeks later the crack that started at a via barrel or a capacitor termination shows up as an intermittent fault in the field — and it is attributed to soldering, not to the split. The cost is not the board: it is the assembly, the freight, the customer's downtime and the warranty claim.

02

A V-cut blade cannot follow a curve

Straight-blade separators handle V-grooved rectangular panels well — that is what they are for. The moment the outline curves, the tabs are on a stamp hole, or the profile is irregular, the blade stops being a process and becomes an operator's judgement call. Routing was invented for exactly those outlines: a small milling cutter follows the path you draw, which is why the published document lists curves, arcs, ellipses, polylines and helices as supported motion.

03

Skilled hands are a capacity risk, not a cost line

Hand separation looks cheap because the labour is already on the payroll. Read the published comparison again: separating by hand is roughly 60 seconds per A4 panel, quality depends on operator intuition, training skilled workers carries a high time cost, and the dust makes the job hard to staff. When that person leaves, the throughput leaves with them. The 2 to 3 operators the machine releases are the same operators you cannot hire twice.

Where this might not apply to you. If every panel you build is a rectangular V-grooved board with straight rails, a much cheaper straight-blade V-cut separator is the correct purchase, and we will say so. Routing earns its place when the outline curves, when the tabs are on stamp holes, when the profile is irregular, or when a mixed high-mix schedule means you would otherwise buy three dedicated machines.

02 — The cycle

Two stations, one spindle, no waiting on the load

The published document describes it as dual-station alternating cycle operation: the two fixture stations work left and right in turn. That single design decision is where the throughput numbers come from. On a single-table machine the spindle stops every time a human touches the fixture; on the S300AS the milling path moves to the other table while the first one is being loaded. The operator's hands and the cutter never wait on each other.

1

Load

Place the panel into the product-specific bakelite fixture on the station that is free. Location is mechanical — no measurement, no judgement.

2

Clamp and confirm

The fixture holds the panel rigid. The dust trays under both stations are already in place, so the cut starts in a controlled envelope.

3

Mill the path

The 800 W spindle follows the stored program — points, lines, arcs, circles, curves, polylines, helixes or ellipses — at a travel speed up to 500 mm/s.

4

Swap and repeat

The head moves to the second station while the finished panel is removed from the first. The cycle count and processing timer are on the pendant.

What the operator actually does, in one cycle

01Panel out of station A
02Next panel into station A
03Cutter finishes station B
04Head indexes to station A
05Panel out of station B
06Next panel into station B

Sequence shown is the alternating dual-station cycle described in the S300AS product document. Actual station timing depends on your panel size, path length and feed rate — a sample separation on your own board is the only way to size it.

Cutting head

The spindle does the work; the guides keep it honest

A precision milling cutter in an 800 W spindle travels on sealed guide rods. The seals are not cosmetic: the published document states they prevent dust and debris from entering, which is what keeps the travel accurate over years rather than months. The same spindle is described as eliminating the static generated during PCB cutting, protecting components from discharge damage.

  • 800 W spindle, precision milling cutter
  • Sealed HIWIN guide rods, dust excluded
  • Static generated in the cut is addressed at the spindle
Role on the line: splits populated panels without bending them
Dust extraction

Fibreglass dust is a health issue before it is a housekeeping issue

Routing generates fine dust from the panel substrate. The machine ships with a high-power vacuum collector described as strong in suction and low in noise, fed by upper waste ducting, with a dust collection tray under each of the two fixture stations. If your operators currently tap panels out over a bench, this is the change they will notice first.

06 — Installation

A desktop machine with a five-point checklist

The S300AS runs on a single-phase full-voltage supply, so the electrical work is trivial compared with a reflow oven. What does need planning is where the dust goes, where the panels queue, and whether the operator can reach both stations without walking around the machine. Plan these five items and commissioning is a single shift.

STEP 1

Bench or floor position

The published machine envelope is L 1350 × W 800 × H 1900 mm including the protective cover. Leave clear access on all four sides — at minimum a working aisle at the loading face and enough room at the rear to service the collector and the ducting.

STEP 2

Power

Full voltage AC 110 V ~ 220 V single phase as published. Feed it from a dedicated circuit with a protective earth. Do not share the circuit with a welding set or a large compressor — voltage sag shows up as inaccurate travel long before it shows up as a fault code.

STEP 3

Dust extraction route

The collector sits with the machine, but you still need a plan for the bin: who empties it, how often, and where the substrate dust goes. Route the flexible ducting so it cannot be crushed against a wall or a bench leg.

STEP 4

Panel flow and WIP

Define where panels queue before the machine and where separated boards go after it. The dual-station cycle only delivers its throughput if the operator never has to leave the machine to fetch work or find a tray.

STEP 5

Fixtures and program library

Decide how fixtures are stored and labelled before the second product arrives. With 1000 program sets resident, the machine will remember everything — your changeover time will be decided by whether a human can find the right fixture.

STEP 6

Verification method

Agree before commissioning how you will check the edge — magnification at the tab, a cross-section on the first article, and an ionic contamination check if the assembly is going for conformal coating.

07 — Payback

Two costs come off the bench. Count the one you can measure.

A routing separator is bought against two different costs. The first is straightforward: the labour of the people separating panels by hand. The second is real but harder to invoice — the micro-cracks, the intermittent field faults and the rework the split causes weeks later. This calculator handles the first one with your numbers. The second one is the argument your quality manager already knows how to make.

Method: panels per month = (3600 ÷ seconds per panel) × hours per day × days per month × utilisation. Annual bench labour addressed = operators released × loaded wage × hours × days × 12. Simple payback = machine price ÷ annual labour addressed. The model deliberately ignores rework savings, scrap savings and the value of the floor space the bench occupied — all of which shorten the real number. Use it as a floor, not a forecast.

10 — Insights

Eight reads on separating boards that have to work

What we have learned putting depaneling machines onto EMS floors, written the way we explain it to a customer standing next to the machine: the problem first, a method you can use without buying anything, and the honest numbers. ARTICLE 01Your best operator cannot feel a micro-crack

Boards leave the separation bench looking perfect and fail six weeks later in the field. Here is the invisible cost chain behind hand-snapping, and the three-question check that exposes it on your own floor.

Pick up a panel that has just been snapped apart by hand and look at the tab. It looks clean. Run your thumb along the edge and it feels smooth. This is the moment where a defect is born and no one records it — because the board in your hand is fine.

What is really happening at the tab

Hand separation is a bending operation. To break a tab you apply a moment load until the glass-epoxy gives way. The energy that breaks the tab does not stop at the tab: it travels into the nearest stiff feature — a via barrel, a plated hole, a ceramic capacitor termination, the solder fillet at a connector pin. Those features survive the load the panel was designed for. They do not always survive a load applied by hand, at an angle, at a speed nobody controls.

The result is a crack you cannot see, on a board that passes AOI, passes ICT and passes final inspection. It fails later, under thermal cycling and vibration, and the failure gets attributed to the solder joint or the component. Meanwhile the real cause — an uncontrolled mechanical load at a station with no recipe — is never investigated, because the station looks like a bench with two people at it.

A check you can run this week

You do not need equipment to find out whether this is happening to you. Ask three questions and listen to the answers.

  • Is there a written setting for the separation step? If the answer names a person rather than a parameter, the process is in someone's wrist.
  • Can two operators produce the same edge? Take ten panels separated by three different people and inspect the tab edges side by side under magnification. Any visible variation means the stress at the tab varied too.
  • Does the field failure history cluster? Sort your warranty returns by board family and look for failures near the panel edge. A cluster that follows the outline is a separation signature, not a soldering signature.

Where the machine changes the answer

A routing separator replaces an impulse with a cut. The S300AS carries a precision milling cutter in an 800 W spindle and removes a thin path of material along the line you programmed, at a feed you set, to a repeatability published at ±0.02 mm. Nothing is loaded in bending, because nothing is being broken — the material is being machined away. The static that builds up at the cutter during PCB separation is addressed at the spindle, which matters when the assembly in front of it is populated.

Why it keeps working after the novelty wears off

A process only holds if it is easier to follow than to bypass. That is why the program library matters more than the spindle spec. With 1000 program sets resident, the operator's correct action is to select the product and load the fixture — not to reach for a tool because the setup is annoying. The right behaviour is the fast behaviour, which is the only reason a process survives a busy Tuesday.

Your next step

Send us one populated panel and the outline drawing. We will separate a sample, photograph the tab edge under magnification and tell you what we see — including when the answer is that your current V-cut process is fine and you should be buying nothing.

ARTICLE 02Sixty seconds a panel is a number somebody guessed

Every quote for a depaneling machine runs on a cycle time. Most of those cycle times were never measured. Here is how to build one you can defend to your own finance team.

Ask three EMS engineers how long it takes to separate one of their panels and you will get three different answers, usually delivered with confidence, usually unmeasured. The number is remembered from a line trial, or inherited from whoever wrote the original process sheet, or simply assumed because it sounded reasonable.

Where the guessed number costs you

A cycle time feeds every important decision downstream. It sets your capacity plan, your labour budget, your quotation, and the payback case for any equipment you buy. If the input is a guess, the confidence in the output is false confidence — the most expensive kind, because it survives review. A machine bought on a guessed cycle time either sits idle or becomes a bottleneck, and in both cases the person who approved it cannot explain what went wrong.

Measure the split, not the station

The mistake is timing the operation instead of the constraint. At a manual bench the constraint is rarely the separation itself; it is the handling around it — sorting panels out of a magazine, stacking separated boards, clearing waste, waiting for a shared tool. Time the whole loop, not the wrist.

  • Time 20 consecutive panels, not 3. The first few are always fast because someone is watching.
  • Include the handling. Start the clock when the operator reaches for the first panel and stop when the last board is in the tray.
  • Record the operator. If two operators produce times that differ by more than 15 %, you have measured a skill, not a process.
  • Note the panel variant. A4, six-up and a 400 mm curved rail are three different products and deserve three different numbers.

What a defensible number looks like

Southern Machinery published a comparison using an A4-sized board: approximately 60 seconds per panel by hand, approximately 30 seconds on the machine, roughly 60 against 120 panels per hour, with 2 to 3 operators released and a 0.002 failure rate. Take that as the vendor's starting point, not as your answer. Your outline length, tab count, material thickness and feed rate all move the number, and only a timed run on your own panel settles it.

Make the number repeatable, not impressive

A machine that produces the same result every shift is worth more than one that produces a hero number once. The S300AS stores 1000 program sets and repeats the path to ±0.02 mm, which means shift two runs the same way shift one did — the condition under which a cycle time is a fact rather than an anecdote. The alternating dual-station cycle is what keeps the spindle busy while the operator handles panels, and that is where the published throughput comes from.

Why the measurement habit outlasts the machine

Once you have a timed baseline for one product, you have a template. The next product takes ten minutes to baseline, and the one after that five. Six months in, you can answer "what will this cost us per panel" without leaving your desk — and that is a capability, not a purchase.

Your next step

Time 20 panels at your current bench this week. Bring the number to us along with the outline drawing, and we will tell you what the S300AS does against it — or where it will not help.

ARTICLE 03Four questions that tell you whether your split is a process

A four-question audit you can run at the depaneling station in fifteen minutes, with no equipment and no purchase. If the station fails two of them, the fix costs less than the failures.

Walk to your depaneling station and stand there for one full panel. Do not ask questions yet. Watch where the operator's hands go, where the waste goes, and whether the next panel is already within reach.

What the fifteen minutes usually reveals

Most depaneling stations are not badly run. They are undesigned. Somebody placed a bench where there was space, put the tools that were available on it, and the operation grew around that. Nobody ever wrote down what the station is supposed to do, so nobody can tell whether it is doing it. The symptom is a station that works perfectly until the day it does not.

The four questions

  • 1. What is the written specification? Not the work instruction that describes the motion — the specification for the result. Tab width after separation, acceptable burr, edge roughness, the magnification at which it is inspected. If this exists, you have a process. If it does not, you have an activity.
  • 2. What controls the result? Name the parameter that changes the outcome. Feed rate, depth of cut, blade condition, fixture location. Then ask whether anyone adjusts it, whether there is a window, and whether the window is recorded anywhere.
  • 3. How do you know it worked? Not "it looks fine." A named check, at a named magnification, by a named role, at a named frequency. If the answer is confidence, you have no feedback loop and therefore no process control.
  • 4. What happens when it fails? Ask what the corrective action was the last time a bad edge was found. If the answer is "we were more careful for a while," the corrective action was a mood.

Turning the answers into a method

Two or more failures on that list means you do not need a new machine first — you need a specification and a fixture. Write the result spec, name the parameter, and set the check. Then measure whether the existing method can hold the spec at all. Often it can, and you have spent nothing. Where it cannot, the audit has told you exactly what the new equipment has to deliver: a controllable feed, a fixed fixture location, and a repeatable path.

What to look for in the equipment

The S300AS maps onto those three requirements. A programmed path fixes the geometry and keeps it fixed across shifts, published at ±0.02 mm repeatability. A product-specific bakelite fixture fixes the location, so the panel cannot shift under the cutter. And a defined feed on an 800 W spindle turns a judgement call into a number. The enclosed cutting envelope with the vacuum collector removes the variable most audits miss — how close to the operator the dust actually gets.

Why the audit is worth repeating

Run the same four questions every quarter, on the same station, and record the answers. The value is not the first audit — it is the trend. A process that quietly loosens between audits is exactly the failure mode that a single inspection will never catch, and a written quarterly answer is the cheapest control you will ever install.

Your next step

Run the four questions at your station and send us the answers. We will tell you which of the four is causing the most scrap at your line, and whether equipment is the fix or a written specification is.

ARTICLE 04Straight blade, stamp hole, curved rail: match the split to the panel

Buying the wrong class of separator is more expensive than buying nothing. A decision tree for choosing between V-cut blades, routing, multi-cutters and vision depaneling — including when the cheap machine is the right answer.

There are four ways to take a panel apart, and the industry sells them all. The mistake is not picking a bad machine — it is picking the machine for the wrong panel geometry, then compensating with operator skill until the volume grows and the compensation stops working.

Why the wrong class fails quietly

A straight V-cut blade on a curved outline does not announce its unsuitability. It cuts approximately along the curve for a while, produces an edge the operator accepts, and generates a slow yield drag that never appears as a single dramatic failure. Nobody quarantines a whole lot over a slightly ragged edge, so the machine earns a reputation for being "fine" while the rework quietly accumulates. Six months later, throughput per operator is worse than the specification promised and nobody can point at the cause.

Decide by outline, then by volume

  • Rectangular, straight V-grooved, high volume. A straight-blade V-cut separator. It is the lowest cost per cut and it is the correct answer. Models like the S-D500 series exist for exactly this job, and buying routing here wastes money.
  • Curved, irregular, or stamp-hole tabs, low to medium volume. A routing separator with a programmed path. This is the S300AS class: a milling cutter follows the outline you drew instead of a line the blade can reach.
  • Same geometry, high volume, floor space for a full machine. An automatic routing separator with servo axes, CCD alignment, a safety door and automatic load and unload — the S380A or S-D4500 class.
  • Very high volumes of small parts, or flexible circuits. A multi-cutter or a vision depaneling machine — the SD5140 and SF680 class. Vision is not about quality here, it is about locating a flexible or low-contrast part that a fixture cannot hold well enough.

The mixed-schedule problem

High-mix factories hit a different constraint than high-volume ones. If you build forty different products a month, dedicating a machine per outline is impossible and buying an automatic router for a panel that appears twice is worse. What you need is one machine that changes product quickly. That is the argument for the S300AS: 1000 program sets resident, a fixture per product, DXF or PLT import with automatic path optimisation, and a changeover measured in fixture plus program rather than in setup hours.

Where the S300AS earns its place — and where it does not

Choose it when the outline curves, when the tabs are on stamp holes, when the profile is irregular, or when a mixed schedule would otherwise need three dedicated machines. Do not choose it when every panel is a rectangular V-grooved board and the volume is high — a straight-blade machine will do that job for a fraction of the cost, and the published cutting range of 600/400/400/100 mm is fixed, so panels outside that envelope need a different conversation entirely.

Keeping the decision good as the product mix moves

Product mixes drift. The panel that made a V-cut machine correct three years ago may be a minority of your volume now. Keep the decision under review by tracking the proportion of your volume that is straight-V-cut against the total. When curved and irregular boards pass roughly a third of the volume, a routing separator starts to pay for the floor space it occupies — and because the S300AS keeps 1000 programs resident, adding the next product costs a fixture, not a machine.

Your next step

ARTICLE 05What ±0.02 mm actually buys you over four thousand panels

Repeatability is the least glamorous number on a specification sheet and the only one that decides whether your second year of production matches your first. A worked example on a 4,000-panel month.

Nobody buys a machine because of the repeatability figure. They buy it because of the spindle, the speed, the footprint or the price, and the repeatability line gets skimmed. Then they run four thousand panels a month for two years and discover which of those numbers they should have read first.

What the number is really protecting

Repeatability is not about how accurately you can cut once — it is about how much the cut varies between panel one and panel four thousand. Every source of drift in a machine shows up here: a guide that has ingested dust, a belt that has stretched, a spindle mount that has moved a fraction under load, a fixture that has worn its location. A machine without a tight repeatability figure hides all of those behind "it looks fine," right up to the shift where it does not.

Run the arithmetic on your own month

Take a 4,000-panel month. If the tab width that protects your board edge has a tolerance window of 0.5 mm and your machine drifts 0.15 mm across a production run, you have consumed nearly a third of your margin by machine behaviour alone — before any fixture wear or operator variation is added. The boards do not fail. They just get progressively closer to the limit, and one day a combination of drift, a slightly worn fixture and a thicker panel crosses it. That is how a "sudden" quality problem is born, and it is never sudden.

  • Published repeatability of the S300AS is ±0.02 mm. Against the example above, that is roughly 4 % of your window rather than 30 %, which leaves the rest of the margin for fixture wear and panel variation.
  • Sealed guide rods support that figure. The published document states the guide rods are sealed to keep dust and debris out, protecting spindle life and performance. A repeatability specification means nothing if the mechanism that delivers it is open to the material you are cutting.
  • Fixture location is the other half. Repeatability of the head is wasted if the panel sits differently every time. The product-specific bakelite fixture removes that variable by design.

Turn the tolerance into a maintenance trigger

Repeatability becomes useful when you convert it into an inspection interval. Measure the tab width on your first article, then on articles at fixed intervals through the run. Plot the trend. When the measured value moves further than a set fraction of the published repeatability away from its first-article value, you have a service signal — you inspect the guides and the fixture instead of waiting for a customer to find the drift.

Why this keeps paying in year three

The argument for a stable machine is not the first year, when everything is new and nothing has drifted. It is the third year, when a machine that holds its geometry is still producing first-article-quality panels while a machine that has quietly loosened is being compensated for by an operator who has learned which way to lean on the fixture. The maintenance position in the published document — over one year for the whole machine, over two years for the spindle, with 3000 hours of spindle maintenance in the period — exists so the trend you record is a maintenance schedule rather than a surprise.

Your next step

Send us the tab-width tolerance from your panel drawing and your monthly volume. We will show you the arithmetic on your own numbers and tell you what the published ±0.02 mm leaves you to spend on fixture wear.

ARTICLE 06The dust you cannot see is the rework you cannot explain

Fibreglass dust is a staffing problem before it is a cleanliness problem, and a contamination problem before it is a cosmetic one. What routing dust does to populated assemblies, and how extraction is specified properly.

Look at the bench after a shift of hand separation. If there is a visible haze of dust on the surface, remember that the particles you can see are the coarse fraction. The fraction that matters for assembly cleanliness and for human lungs is the one that has already settled everywhere else in the room.

Two separate problems wearing one coat

The first problem is the people. The published efficiency comparison states it plainly: the dust generated makes the job undesirable for many workers, and training skilled workers carries a high time cost. If your separation bench is hard to staff, treat that as a technical finding rather than a management one. The second problem is the product. Deposited dust on a populated assembly is contamination, and on a board heading for conformal coating it is a coating adhesion defect waiting to happen.

Specify extraction as a system, not a vacuum

  • Capture at the cut, not at the bench. Extraction that pulls from the room is housekeeping. Extraction that pulls from the cutting envelope is process control. The S300AS routes waste ducting directly from the cutting area.
  • Collect under the work, not just beside it. Two dust recovery trays sit under the two fixture stations, so material that falls through is captured rather than redistributed.
  • Enclose the envelope. The sheet-metal environmentally protective cover is listed as a standard build item. It contains dust and reduces noise at the same time, which is why it should not be treated as an accessory.
  • Match suction to noise. The published description is strong suction with low noise. That combination is the whole point — an extraction system your operators switch off because it screams is a system that is not running.

Close the loop on the bin

Extraction only works if the collected material leaves the machine. Name who empties the bin, set the interval from real fill rate rather than from the manual, and check the ducting for crushing or disconnection at the same time. A collapsed flexible duct is the most common reason an extraction system stops working while the vacuum still sounds healthy.

Why the same design also protects the components

Routing generates static as the cutter works the substrate. The published document states the high-precision cutting spindle is designed to eliminate the static generated during PCB cutting, protecting components and preventing chip burnout from discharge. That matters most when the assembly in front of the cutter is already populated and already paid for — which, at the depaneling station, it always is.

Why extraction keeps earning after the installation

A clean bench changes who is willing to work at it, and staffing stability shows up in yield long after the machine is forgotten. That is the quiet return on an extraction system: it is not a feature on the machine, it is a reason the process does not depend on a small number of people who tolerate the environment.

Your next step

Send us a photograph of your current separation station at the end of a shift. We will tell you what the dust pattern is telling you, and what extraction would have to capture to change it.

ARTICLE 07From drawing to first good panel in one shift

A setup sequence for a desktop routing separator that takes a new product from outline drawing to a verified first article without waiting for a specialist visit.

The reason new equipment sits idle for weeks is rarely mechanical. It is that the path from "machine installed" to "machine producing good parts" was never written down, so it waits for the one person who knows how, and that person is busy.

Why the gap is a process gap

Commissioning a router is four decisions and one verification. Made in the right order, it is a single shift. Made in the wrong order — programming before the fixture is approved, or cutting before the process window is set — it becomes a week of rework and a machine with a reputation for being difficult.

The sequence

  1. Confirm the split line on the drawing. Mark the routing path and the tab widths you need to keep the assembly rigid until the end of the line. This is a design decision and it belongs before any programming.
  2. Approve the fixture. The bakelite fixture locates the panel on both stations. Approve it on a real board, not on a drawing, before you program a path that depends on it.
  3. Program the path. Teach it on the 320 × 240 pendant, or import the DXF or PLT outline and let the controller optimise it. Use the graphic preview to check the path closes and clears every component before you cut anything.
  4. Set the process window before the first production board. Spindle speed, feed, depth of cut and extraction running. The published document describes four wire-drawing process options, per-instruction glue-on delay, glue-off delay and retract height for guidance work — decide these once, record them, and change them only with a reason.
  5. Run one panel and verify the edge. Magnification at the tab, and a cross-section on the first article. If the assembly is going for conformal coating, add an ionic contamination check — contamination from the cutting process is exactly what coating adhesion fails on.
  6. Move to the alternating cycle. Only once the single-panel result is good. Set the production quantity and the processing timer on the pendant, then run both stations so loading happens inside the cut.

What makes it possible without a specialist

The S300AS keeps 1000 program sets resident and can hold hundreds of files on the pendant at up to 8000 instructions each. Parameters download over RS232 for offline standalone operation, so the machine does not need a PC on the bench. The practical effect is that the first product takes a shift and the second takes an hour — because everything the first one taught you is still in the controller.

Why the library is the real asset

Write the process window for every product into a shared record the moment you set it. Two years later, when the machine has thirty products in it and somebody leaves, the record is the difference between a controlled changeover and an afternoon of guessing. The machine remembers the path; only you can remember why the feed was set where it was.

ARTICLE 08A second shift without a second hire

When volume rises, the reflex is to add people. Here is the arithmetic for adding capacity instead — and the honest conditions under which it does not work.

Volume goes up twelve per cent. The plant manager asks for two more operators on the separation bench. The request is reasonable, it is easy to approve, and it quietly raises the fixed cost of the process that is hardest to staff.

Why headcount is the most expensive capacity

Labour added to a manual station is permanent and it scales linearly. Double the volume, double the bench. It also concentrates risk: the published comparison notes that hand separation depends on operator intuition, that training skilled workers carries a high time cost, and that the dust makes the role hard to fill. Adding two people to a station that is already hard to staff does not remove the constraint — it multiplies it.

Run the capacity comparison honestly

Use the published figures as a starting point and then substitute your own. On an A4 panel the comparison is approximately 60 seconds by hand against approximately 30 on the machine, roughly 60 against 120 panels per hour, with 2 to 3 operators released and a 0.002 failure rate. Now apply your reality:

  • Use your measured cycle time, not ours. If your outline is longer than an A4 perimeter, the machine figure moves and so does the payback.
  • Apply a real utilisation. A machine queued with work 75 % of the shift delivers 75 %. Model it that way rather than at 100 %.
  • Count the released operators as redeployed, not deleted. The value is capacity you did not have to hire, and it is real even if nobody is made redundant.
  • Add the quality term separately. A 0.002 failure rate is a published figure for the machine; the field-failure cost of hand separation is a number only your quality team can put on it.

How the machine absorbs the growth

Capacity from equipment does not scale linearly with volume — it scales in steps, and the steps are cheap after the first one. The S300AS holds 1000 program sets, so adding the next product costs a fixture rather than a machine, and the alternating dual-station cycle means the extra volume is absorbed by the cut time rather than by hiring. When volume outgrows a desktop machine entirely, the step up is the automatic separator class — and by then you will know from real numbers, not from a forecast.

The honest condition

This argument only holds if the volume is genuinely there. A machine that runs four hours a shift because the work is not queued is a worse decision than hiring one person. That is why the calculator on this page asks for a utilisation figure and refuses to default to a hundred per cent. If your honest utilisation is under forty per cent, add the person and revisit the question next year.

Why the decision compounds

Every year you avoid adding a body to a hard-to-staff station is a year of staffing risk you did not take on, and that compounds in a way a hire does not. The equipment is also still on the floor in year five, doing the same work at the same rate, which is more than can be said for a bench that depends on who is standing at it.

Your next step

Give us your monthly volume, your measured cycle time and your honest utilisation. We will run the comparison against the published figures and tell you whether the machine or the hire is the better answer — including when the hire is.

13 — FAQ

The questions this machine actually raises

What does the S300AS actually separate?
Curved outlines, V-cut boards, stamp-hole (snap) panels and irregular profiles on populated or unpopulated PCBA. The published document lists switches, mobile phones, tablets, audio systems, POS machines, navigation devices, toys and automotive products as the substrate applications. Because the tool is a milling cutter following a programmed path, it can cut any outline you can draw and close — points, straight lines, arcs, full circles, curves, polylines, helixes and ellipses.
Is this a router or a V-cut machine?
It is a routing separator. A precision milling cutter follows a programmed path and removes a thin strip of material, so the result is a milled edge rather than a sheared one. That is why it handles curved and irregular outlines a straight blade cannot follow, and why it applies no bending stress to the assembly. If every panel you build is a rectangular V-grooved board, a straight-blade machine is cheaper and we will tell you so.
How fast is it against hand-snapping?
Southern Machinery measured an A4-sized panel at approximately 30 seconds on the machine — about 120 panels per hour — against approximately 60 seconds, or 60 panels per hour, separating by hand. The same comparison states 2 to 3 operators released and a 0.002 failure rate. Those are the published figures. Confirm them on your own panel in a sample separation before you plan capacity on them.
Do I need a fixture for every product?
Yes. The bakelite fixture is product specific — it locates the panel and holds it while the cutter travels, and it is the reason the published ±0.02 mm repeatability is achievable in production rather than only on a specification sheet. The machine stores 1000 program sets, so changeover is fixture plus program. Send the outline drawing and the fixture is quoted with the machine.
Can it run offline without a PC at the bench?
Yes. Programs are created by teach programming on the handheld controller or imported from DXF and PLT files with automatic path optimisation, then downloaded over the RS232 interface for offline standalone operation. Parameters can also be saved on the teaching pendant for recall and copied between devices, so the machine does not need a computer beside it.
What keeps the dust out of my assembly area?
The machine ships with a high-power vacuum dust collector described as strong in suction and low in noise, upper waste ducting from the cutting envelope, a dust recovery tray under each of the two fixture stations, and a sheet-metal environmentally protective cover as a standard build item. The published document also states the cutting spindle is designed to eliminate the static generated during PCB cutting, protecting components from discharge damage.
What is the floor footprint?
The published machine envelope is L 1350 × W 800 × H 1900 mm including the protective cover. Plan clear access on all four sides — a working aisle at the loading face, and room at the rear for the collector and ducting. Power is full-voltage AC 110 V ~ 220 V single phase, so no three-phase supply is required.
What is the lead time and what is in the scope?
Standard scope is one S300AS desktop router separator, the handheld teaching controller, one product fixture built to your outline, the dust collector, tooling and documentation. Free sample separation, one year of free warranty service and free technical training, process guidance and production-import support are published inclusions. Lead time and price are confirmed per order once the fixture and the panel volume are known.
